doc.title: Vincent Pelote interviewed by Monk Rowe, Orlando, Florida, February 25, 2017

chapter: Henderson, Goodman and the swing era
title: Writing the 'Fragments' column and the Henderson versus Goodman question
summary: As a college student Pelote wrote a trivia column for Jazz Magazine, admitting some questions were plants, and regrets a tirade about why Goodman succeeded with Henderson's arrangements; he now knows Goodman supported Henderson.

story.theme_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the leader and his bands
story.community_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the perfectionist bandleader

blocks.x: Yeah. There was a — I was doing a little poking around about you.
There was a magazine, you wrote, maybe it was a column, answers to your jazz history questions.
Oh no. Jazz Magazine out of Northport, New York. “Fragments” was the column.
Did you get — what kind of questions did people ask you?

All right. I was very young at the time, okay? In fact Chris White was the director at the time, so we are talking ’74, ’75. I was still in college, wet behind the ears just really sort of getting into the whole jazz thing. And the kind of questions that were sent were sort of like — I guess you call them trivia questions now you know. What recording did Rahsaan Roland Kirk play a sarrusophone on or some things like that. Also I will confess now that the magazine is defunct that some of those questions were plants. I asked my brother to ask me a question and I would put it in, or I would ask a friend to send me a question or ask me a question and I would include it. Because I didn’t want to just make up something. I figured so at least I could say legitimately that somebody asked me this, they at least sent it in. Because we had to have a column and sometimes nothing was coming in. We weren’t getting any people writing anything in. And I will admit there was one question that I wish to this day I could do over again, the answer. It was about Fletcher Henderson versus Benny Goodman. You know, why was Goodman successful playing the exact same arrangements that Fletcher Henderson played. And I was sort of into my — how can I put this — I was sort of into my black nationalist bag at that time, which believe me I’m nowhere a black nationalist in any way, shape or form, but at that time I was sort of sniffing around in that area. And of course I launched into this whole tirade about how well yes, the black musicians were treated like crap and Fletcher, his music was twenty times better than Benny Goodman’s, but because he was black — of course I didn’t know or was aware until much, much later was that Henderson was paid very well for those arrangements, he was paid probably better than most arrangers were getting at that time, and Goodman loved him. Goodman considered him like a second father, really. And really took him in when he disbanded his band in ’34 and put him basically on the payroll and just had him turn out charts for him. A lot of them he didn’t even use, he just put them in the library and never got back to performing them or recording them, but he gave the guy a steady gig. And then when their band disbanded later, when Fletcher re-formed and then disbanded later, Goodman took him back in the organization and that’s how he ends up on those Charlie Christian-Goodman things as the pianist, even though he had a perfectly good pianist in the band, Jess Stacy, who he didn’t use on any of those recordings. He gave them to Fletcher Henderson instead. I love the guy but his piano playing at that point was really very old fashioned, out of step.
